## Why Dirty Fuel Tanks Destroy Connectors and Pumps

Replacing fuel pumps on a 2009 Dodge Charger SRT8 is an expensive endeavor, especially when the new units fail shortly after installation. It is easy to fall into the trap of assuming a component failure is purely electrical or mechanical without looking deeper at the environment in which that component operates. In your specific case, the diagnosis points away from a catastrophic alternator or battery issue and toward a more insidious culprit: a contaminated fuel tank.

The visual evidence you providedâthe burned corner pin on both fuel pump connectorsâis the smoking gun here. When you see arcing or burning on a connector pin, it usually indicates a momentary loss of ground continuity combined with high current draw. While electrical noise from an alternator can cause issues, it rarely burns pins repeatedly unless there is an underlying resistance problem preventing proper current flow.

The root cause lies in the fuel itself. Fuel pumps are designed to move liquid hydrocarbons, but they are not immune to particulate matter. Over time, older gas tanks accumulate sludge, rust flakes, and degraded rubber gaskets. This debris settles at the bottom of the tank, directly where the pump sits. When you install a new pump into this environment, the intake screen immediately begins clogging.

This clogging forces the fuel pump motor to work significantly harder to maintain the required pressure for the engine. As the resistance increases, the voltage drop across the motor rises. If the resistance becomes high enough, the motor draws excessive amperage (over-current). This excess current generates intense heat within the small connector housing. Once that heat exceeds the rating of the plastic insulation or the solder joint, you get the burning and melting you observed on the pins.

The fact that this happened to two different pumps confirms that the issue was systemic, not a defect in the pump units themselves. The fuel tank likely contained enough debris to clog the new intake screens within weeks or months, triggering the same overheating cycle twice. The black filter material you found inside the pump assembly is physical proof of this; it indicates a massive amount of particulate matter had bypassed any initial filtration and entered the pump housing itself.

You mentioned that your alternator, battery, and relay tests were normal. That effectively rules out the power supply side as the primary failure point. A weak battery might cause starting issues, but it wouldn't burn connector pins on a high-load accessory like a fuel pump unless the alternator was failing to compensateâa scenario you have already excluded. The cable management you plan to improve is also a good preventive measure, ensuring that external vibrations or chafing don't exacerbate the connection issue, though the internal contamination is the primary driver of the burnout.

Your strategy to return to the original garage for a proper tank cleaning and replacement is the correct path forward. However, be aware that simply "cleaning" an old tank often misses the point. If the tank has been in service for years, the interior coating may have degraded, or rust may still be flaking off. A thorough flush using a high-volume pump to remove sludge and replace the fuel filter is essential before reinstalling any new hardware.

Regarding your question on whether dirt alone can burn a pin: strictly speaking, dirt does not generate heat. However, dirt creates the conditions for electrical failure. By restricting flow, dirt causes the motor to overwork, leading to overheating. The resulting thermal expansion and vibration then compromise the connector's contact resistance. This high resistance turns any normal operating current into enough heat to melt plastic and burn pins. It is an indirect but definitive causal chain.

When you order a new fuel pump for the Charger SRT8, ensure that you also inspect the fuel pump relay and wiring harness for any signs of heat damage or melted insulation near the connector points. Even if they appear intact now, the previous failures suggest the thermal environment was extreme. If the tank cleaning is not performed with high diligence, the new pump will likely face the same fate as its predecessors, wasting more money on repairs.
